findings.title: `continue` inside `for i in lo..hi` (and C-style `for`) restarts the loop without running the step: infinite loop
findings.why: The range form is desugared into `while i < hi { { user-body } i += 1 }`: the step is the LAST statement of the while body, so a `continue` in the body jumps straight to the loop condition and the increment is never executed. Nothing downstream repairs it: `forDesugar` (parser.c:2465) is only read by check_stmt.c:201, and that retargeting only rewrites for-each-over-iterator loops (it drops the step and advances via `next()`); the same step-at-end shape is produced for the C-style form at parser.c:2343 and for the for-each form at parser.c:2457. The generated C proves the mechanism: `while (i < 5) { if (i == 2) { continue; } sum += i; i += 1; }`.
findings.trigger: Any `for` loop whose body can reach a `continue` before the loop variable passes the bound, e.g. `for i in 0..5 { if i == 2 { continue } sum += i }`. Same for `for (var i = 0; i < 5; i += 1) { if i == 2 { continue } ... }`.

findings.title: `p->sawBuiltin` is parser-global, not per-declaration: a second `@builtin` in a struct/impl body is falsely rejected, and the first is silently ignored
findings.why: The flag means "this declaration already said @builtin", but it is stored on the Parser, which parses the whole file. It is reset only on the module-level `fn` path (parser.c:797 `p.sawBuiltin = false;`, immediately before parseFunc). parseStruct (parser.c:887) and parseImpl (parser.c:1220) call parseFuncAnnotations without ever resetting it and without an out-parameter for `@builtin` at all, so: (a) the second `@builtin` method in the file is rejected with an error that names the wrong declaration ("appears twice on the same function"), and (b) the first one is accepted with a body and then silently dropped (no isBuiltin is set on a method), which contradicts the file's own rule that an annotation must never be silently ignored (parser.c:1442-1446).
findings.trigger: Two `@builtin`-annotated methods anywhere in one file (struct body or impl block).

findings.title: Function type parameters are not checked to start uppercase, so `fn f<point>(p: point)` silently shadows the struct `point`
findings.why: parseTypeDecl (parser.c:1277) and parseStruct (parser.c:863) both enforce `startsUpper` on type parameters, and the comment at parser.c:1335-1343 states the invariant ("the two sets are disjoint and a type parameter can never collide with a type name"). parseFunc's generic list relies on the comment instead of a check, so a lowercase type parameter is accepted and shadows a real type name for the whole body and signature. Consequence measured: with `struct point` declared, `fn f<point>(p: point)` becomes generic over any type and `f(3)` type-checks, while the identical name in `struct holder<point>` is rejected as an error.
findings.trigger: A function type parameter that is not uppercase, most damaging when it is the name of an existing type (loophole the struct/type paths close).

findings.title: `at()` only refuses string-vs-punctuation matches, so a statement-position string literal that spells a keyword is taken for that keyword
findings.why: at() (parser.c:68-72) guards the text comparison only when the compared spelling is punctuation (`if (t->kind == TK_STRING && lexIsPunct(value)) return false;`). For keyword spellings it compares text alone, and a string token stores its contents without quotes, so a TK_STRING whose text is `yield` compares equal to the keyword. parseStmt dispatches on at(p, "yield"/"let"/"var"/"if"/"while"/"for"/"trap"/"match"/"return"/"break"/"continue") before ever reaching parseExpr, so a bare string expression statement is misparsed. `"abc"` as a statement compiles; `"yield"` dies in the yield branch with a message about a keyword the user never wrote.
findings.trigger: An expression statement consisting of a single string literal whose contents are exactly a keyword spelling.
findings.repro:
printf 'fn main() -> i32 {
    "abc"
    return 0
}
' > /tmp/t_ok.extc   # exit 0
printf 'fn main() -> i32 {
    "yield"
    return 0
}
' > /tmp/t_kw.extc  # exit 1
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc /tmp/t_ok.extc; echo $?
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc /tmp/t_kw.extc; echo $?
# -> t_kw.extc:2:5: error: `yield` needs a value: `yield expr`
# same for "let" (expected a variable name) and "match" (expected an expression)

findings.title: Fixed-array length has no upper bound: `[9223372036854775807]i32` type-checks and the generated C is rejected by cc
findings.why: The only validation of `[N]T` is positivity, although N is an i64 literal. The checker accepts it and codegen emits `int32_t data[9223372036854775807];`; cc then refuses the file (`size of array ... exceeds maximum object size`). Without --check-c the driver happily prints C that cannot build, which breaks the promise stated at main.c:322-325 ("a program which type-checks will build"). With --check-c the diagnostic is the internal-error message "the generated C does not compile -- this is an extc bug", which blames the compiler for a source-level absurdity.
findings.trigger: Any fixed array whose length is large enough that the element size times the count exceeds what the C compiler accepts (repro uses i64 max; [2305843009213693952]i32 also fails).
findings.repro:
printf 'fn main() -> i32 {
    var a: [9223372036854775807]i32
    return 0
}
' > /tmp/t_big.extc
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc /tmp/t_big.extc --check-c; echo $?
# -> exit 1, cc: size of array 'data' exceeds maximum object size
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc /tmp/t_big.extc | grep 'int32_t data'   # invalid C emitted anyway

findings.title: `effects` clause rejects `Ret` when it is not the first key (`effects Addr=0 Ret=0`), although `effects Ret=0 Addr=0` is accepted
findings.why: parseEffectsClause loops over `name = int` pairs, and after each pair decides whether another key follows by testing only Addr/Cont/Thread. `Ret` (handled at parser.c:360-372) is missing, so the loop stops right after a pair that precedes `Ret`, leaving `Ret=0` to be parsed as the next top-level declaration. `effects Ret=0 Addr=0` works because Addr is in the test; `effects Addr=0 Ret=0` (equally legal, same clause) fails with "expected `fn`, `struct`, `type`, `let` or `var`, found `Ret`", which points at the key, not at the ordering rule. parseFunc (parser.c:1619 for no-body declarations, parser.c:1634 for functions with a body) is the caller inside this unit's range; the defective line itself sits at 392, just below the assigned range.
findings.trigger: Writing `Ret=` after any other effect key, in an `extern!` declaration or in an `effects` clause on a function with a body.
findings.repro:
printf 'extern!("libc") fn f1(p: ref u8) -> i32 effects Addr=0 Ret=0
fn main() -> i32 { return 0 }
' > /tmp/t_A.extc
printf 'extern!("libc") fn f2(p: ref u8) -> i32 effects Ret=0 Addr=0
fn main() -> i32 { return 0 }
' > /tmp/t_B.extc
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc /tmp/t_A.extc; echo $?  # -> 1, 'found `Ret`'
/home/alphayang/extC_Compiler/build/extc /tmp/t_B.extc; echo $?  # -> 0

findings.title: C-style `for (init; cond; step)` cannot omit the init or the step, although the parser documents the C shape
findings.why: All three sections of the C-style header are parsed unconditionally: parseStmt for the initializer (2327) and parseStmt for the step (2335), with parseExpr for the condition (2331). An empty section is therefore not an empty statement but a parse error from the middle of an expression, even though the desugaring comment at parser.c:2264 documents the form as `for (init; cond; step) -> { init while cond { { B } step } }`, where an empty init or step is trivially expressible. The two idioms `for (; p != null; p = p.next)` and `for (i = 0; i < n; )` are rejected with "expected an expression, found `;`" / "found `)`".
findings.trigger: Omitting the initializer or the step in the C-style for header.

coverage_notes: Read src/parser.c 1221-2440 line by line (all of it, no sampling). Functions covered: tail of the parseImpl member loop (1221-1250); parseTypeDecl (1259-1330, incl. optional leading `|`, payload types, type-parameter case check); startsUpper (1333); expectTypeName (1344-1356); expectFuncName (1368-1417, operator fusion for ==,!=,<,<=,>,>=,+,-,*,/,%, <<,>>, [],[],=); parseFuncAnnotations (1451-1552); parseFunc (1554-1650, type params, params, return type, noBody/extern and @builtin paths, effects-on-body rejection rules); parseType (1663-1804, dyn/mut/?/ref/[N]T/fn-type/qualified+generic names); parseFnType (1818-1847); parseBlock (1856-1872); parseMatch (1886-1958); parseStmt (1966-2105, @overwrite, yield, let/var, if/while/for, trap-by-shape, match, return/break/continue, nested-decl rejection, trailing-domain block, compound assignment, `x = yield`); parseGlobalDecl (2115-2146); parseVarDecl (2156-2208, incl. `var x = yield`); parseIf (2216-2241); for-desugar helpers forIdent/forInt/forStep/forBlock/forRepeatable (2279-2318); parseFor all four forms (2320-2440). Cross-checked and found NOT to be defects: startsUpper is forward-declared at 180 (no implicit declaration); typeNamed allocates a fresh node per call, so filling ty->targs/mut/nullable cannot alias a shared type; parseGlobalDecl's documented "initializer must be a literal" is enforced by the checker (`var g = f()` -> "the global `g` must be initialized with a constant"); zero-init for a missing initializer and the `@overwrite`-on-`let` case are both re-rejected by the checker; `for` desugaring names (`__extc_s`, `__extc_i`) cannot collide with user names because lexIdent rejects any identifier starting with `__` (lexer.c:268-272, verified by test); the for-each element copy (`mut=false`) and the half-open range are documented and behave as documented; parseMatch's unchecked `arm->body = parseBlock(p)` at 1944 cannot be observed because ctxError is fatal and the driver stops before any later pass (tested with an unterminated arm: clean error, no crash/hang). The `continue` defect of the range/C-style forms is reported here (line 2394 and, in the same shape, 2343); the for-each variant is reported in parser-3.json against line 2457. One finding (line 392) is just below the assigned range and is included because parseFunc in this range is its only caller; the audit of 1-1220 may report the same line. One more unit-1 finding was added after the first pass: the C-style for header rejects empty init/step sections (line 2327/2335, repro /tmp/t_for3.extc and /tmp/t_for4.extc). Also noted but deliberately NOT reported: `looksLikeAssoc` misreads `a < b > (c)` as the generic call `a<b>(c)` (error message: "`a` is not a built-in primitive or generic function"), but both readings are rejected for valid programs, so no accept/reject decision changes; `@inline`/`@builtin` written twice in a row at top level are accepted without the duplicate check that the same annotations get elsewhere (parser.c:515-518 and 578-584, outside this range).
